newsitem.title: BULGARIA: NEW PROTESTS ADD TO PRESSURE ON BULGARIA SOCIALISTS.
newsitem.headline: NEW PROTESTS ADD TO PRESSURE ON BULGARIA SOCIALISTS.

text.p: Fresh strikes and rallies added to pressure on Bulgaria's ruling Socialists on Thursday but they seemed no closer to agreement with the opposition on forming a new government.
As protests fuelled by economic hardship reached their 11th consecutive day, four leading reformists left the party and an opinion poll put its public support at just eight percent.

Schools, hospitals and factories held protests ranging from one-hour warning strikes and rallies to symbolic wearing of blue protest ribbons. Some workers at the Stomana steelworks in Pernik, near Sofia, held a rally and stopped work for an hour.
About 2,000 students marched past the presidency in their daily protest and President Zhelyu Zhelev came out to shake their hands. He invited student leaders in for talks.
Some 15,000 people, more than on Wednesday, attended a rally and concert outside Sofia's gold-domed cathedral.

"I can promise you that we will never again allow another Socialist government to rule this country because we do not want chaos to prevail over democracy any more," Nedezhda Mihailova, spokeswoman of the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), told the rally.
A march and rally in the pro-government stronghold of Kozloduy won scant support from well-paid workers at the town's nuclear plant.

UDF leader Ivan Kostov was in the northern town of Silistra to give support to the UDF candidate in a municipal election and negotiations to allow formation of a new government showed no sign of progress, though the Socialist leadership was meeting on Thursday afternoon.
The Socialists plan a broad-based interim government of technocrats to rule until elections but insist it must be led by their nominee for premier, Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev.
The Socialists' parliamentary leader Krassimir Premyanov said he hoped the so-called "programme government" would enjoy broad parliamentary support.

"It is of the utmost importance to have a government which will continue negotiations with the IMF as soon as possible and technically such a government would achieve this fastest," he told national radio. "In this crisis, Bulgaria cannot be ruled by a single party."

Reformists Andrei Raichev, Rossen Karadimov, Dimitar Yonchev and Andrei Bundjulov said they were leaving the Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) because it had failed to adapt to the demands of the post-communist era.

"I think all the people in the streets have a right to protest because the BSP made too many mistakes. We think the best option for Bulgaria is immediate elections and no interim government," Yonchev said.
The Socialists have suggested holding elections by December, a year ahead of schedule.
The UDF says it is ready for talks but does not want a new Socialist government be formed under the present parliament -- implying parliamentary polls sooner than the government offers.

An opinion poll by the MBMD polling agency, published in the daily Novinar, showed that while the Socialists' support had fallen drastically, UDF support had not changed since November's presidential elections.
"This supports the thesis that the people are on the streets not for political motives but for purely economic ones," said MBMD director Mira Yanova.

The Socialists won parliamentary elections in December 1994 but last November's presidential election was won by opposition lawyer Petar Stoyanov, who will be sworn in on Sunday and formally takes office on Wednesday.
Zhelev, a staunch critic of the BSP, has refused to ask the party to form a new government in the present atmosphere. The task is likely to be handed on to Stoyanov next week.
